judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same statement-type grain, rank 0) under STRAND 4: WRITING, so any direction needs substantive evidence rather than shared ancestry, weak code-prefix overlap ('b1','4'), or shared tokens ('write','using'). The substantive difference is unit of production: B1.4.3.1.3 (Sub-Strand 3, Writing Letters – Small and Capital; standard B1.4.3.1 'use general skills strategies and knowledge of letter sounds to write legibly and boldly') asks pupils to write words correctly using capital and small letters, whereas B1.4.7.1.2 (Sub-Strand 7, Controlled Writing; standard B1.4.7.1 'Write simple compositions') asks pupils to produce a connected simple composition from a substitution table. Reliable word-level transcription with correct capital/small letter use supports success in composing and writing out sentences into a simple composition, so proficiency in the first plausibly supports the second within the same grade. Evidence is bounded: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and only indicator text plus hierarchy is available, which limits certainty about explicit sequencing.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same grain, same resolved rank 0) about characters in a story, but they differ substantively in cognitive demand and scope. B1.1.7.1.3 (Oral Language / Listening Comprehension) is 'Recognise and discuss characters in a story', with LCs 'Identify characters in a story' and 'Discuss characters in a story'. B1.2.7.2.2 (Reading / Comprehension) is 'Describe characters and their actions in a story', whose LC adds the 'actions' dimension and a descriptive, text-based characterisation task. Being able to recognise and talk about who the characters are supports success in describing those characters and what they do; the second extends the first from recognition/oral discussion to elaborated description including character actions within read narrative texts. Same-rank direction is grounded in this substantive expansion of demand (recognise/discuss -> describe characters plus actions), not in shared grade, code prefix, or wording overlap alone. Note the different Strand/Sub-Strand placements (Oral Language/Listening Comprehension vs Reading/Comprehension) and that both endpoints' source evidence is truncated, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement and LC text available.

judgment.rationale: Both are Basic 3 (rank 2) Indicators in Strand 1 Oral Language, Sub-Strand 6 Conversation, so the grain and topic match. B3.1.6.1.2 'Talk about events in the community' sits under the exploratory Content Standard B3.1.6.1 'Explore using certain culturally acceptable language for communication': learners practise sustained oral talk on a concrete familiar topic. B3.1.6.2.3 'Participate in communication, using more varied and more accurate language' sits under B3.1.6.2 'Apply knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation' and explicitly demands comparatively greater lexical variety and accuracy in conversational participation. Competence in topic-based community talk plausibly supports the more demanding, quality-focused application indicator, giving an explore-to-apply developmental direction from second to first rather than mere repeated wording (token overlap was only the word 'in'/'commun-' trigrams and is not the basis of this judgment). Shared ancestry, code prefix, and same-grade proximity were treated as nomination context only. judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicator-grain statements in the same Strand 1: Oral Language / Sub-Strand 4: Story Telling line, under the parallel 'Respond to stories' content standards (B2.1.4.1 and B3.1.4.1). The second SFI (B2.1.4.1.3, 'Tell stories from cultural background', coordinate BASIC 2, rank 1) establishes oral narrative production of known stories; the first SFI (B3.1.4.1.3, 'Create own events to extend stories heard', coordinate BASIC 3, rank 2) requires the learner to go beyond reproducing a heard story to inventing and integrating new episodes into it. That is a pair-specific expansion of capability (retell existing cultural narratives -> generate original narrative material extending a heard story), not mere repeated wording, and competence in telling stories orally plausibly supports success in creatively extending them. Direction is lower-to-higher rank (BASIC 2 to BASIC 3), matching the permitted second_to_first. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted evidence items each), so judgment rests on the statement text, codes, identity scope (grade/strand/sub-strand) and storytelling Learning Component tags actually supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints sit at BASIC 3 (rank 2), so direction rests on substantive content, not rank. The second SFI (B3.2.2.1.1, Reading / Phonics) asks learners to 'Understand the relationship between spelling of words and sounds of speech', under the parent Content Standard 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write' — an explicit link from phonic sound-letter knowledge to writing. The first SFI (B3.4.9.3.2, Writing / Writing as a Process) requires learners to 'Proofread draft to correct punctuation and spelling errors', with a supplied Learning Component 'Proofread draft to correct spelling errors'. Grasping grapheme–phoneme/spelling–sound correspondences plausibly supports the likelihood of success in detecting and correcting misspellings while proofreading one's own draft, so the phonics indicator builds towards the proofreading indicator. The shared evidence is not mere repeated wording: the token overlap ('spelling') is backed by a substantive skill link from decoding/encoding knowledge to applied spelling correction. Note the first indicator also covers punctuation, which the phonics indicator does not support, limiting the scope of the dependency; confidence is moderate accordingly. Source-evidence truncation on both endpoints and LC truncation on the second SFI mean some supporting exemplar text is unavailable.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same grain, same rank 0), so direction rests on substantive content rather than coordinate order. B1.4.3.1.2 (Strand 4 Writing, Sub-Strand 3 'Writing Letters – Small and Capital', under standard B1.4.3.1 on using letter-sound knowledge to write legibly) requires copying names of objects correctly in both upper and lower case letters — i.e. accurate formation of and discrimination between capital and small letter forms. B1.5.1.1.3 (Strand 5 Using Writing Conventions/Grammar Usage, Sub-Strand 1 'Using Capitalisation', under standard B1.5.1.1 'Apply knowledge of capitalisation in writing') requires the learner to decide when a word is a proper noun and write it with a capital letter. Reliable production of upper- vs lower-case letter forms when writing names plausibly supports success at applying the capitalisation convention to proper nouns; the second extends handwriting/case-form control into rule-governed convention use. This is inferred curriculum coherence, not an asserted mandatory prerequisite; the shared token 'letters' and shared BASIC 1 grade ancestor alone were not treated as sufficient. judgment.rationale: Both indicators sit under the same BASIC 3 Content Standard B3.5.4.1 ('Apply knowledge of action words in communication'), Sub-Strand 'Using Action Words', Strand 'Using Writing Conventions/Grammar Usage', and share the same resolved coordinate rank (BASIC 3), so direction cannot rest on grade rank alone. The statement texts give substantive same-rank evidence: B3.5.4.1.2 requires using the present continuous form of verbs to describe actions happening at the time of speaking, while B3.5.4.1.3 requires simple past plus the past continuous form to express past actions. Command of the continuous (be + -ing) construction in the present, evidenced by LC 'Use the present tense continuous form of verbs', supports success with the past continuous, and B3.5.4.1.3 additionally broadens to a new tense (simple past) and to past-time reference (LCs 'Use past continuous forms of verbs to express past actions' and 'Use simple past forms of verbs to express past actions'). This is expanded capability, not mere repeated wording, so the present-continuous indicator builds towards the past-tense indicator (second_to_first). Note that both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source/LC evidence, and the nomination evidence is truncated, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement texts, hierarchy and LCs supplied.

The fluency source context shows the indicator focus on reading texts/stories/passages 'with good pace, accuracy and expression', i.e. accurate automatic oral reading, while the comprehension standard requires applying reading skills and techniques to understand and interpret text meaning (source context references purpose and features of information texts). Within this same-grade pairing the substantive change is from executing accurate, well-paced reading of text to extracting and interpreting meaning from it; proficiency in fluent reading plausibly supports success in understanding and interpreting the same texts, supporting a same-rank developmental direction from the fluency standard to the comprehension standard rather than the reverse. The second (B1.2.2.1.5, Reading/Phonics, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write') asks learners to segment syllables/words into sounds — a phonemic segmentation skill (LC: 'Segment syllables/words into sounds'). Segmenting spoken words into constituent sounds is the encoding-enabling skill that the spelling standard explicitly invokes as 'phonics knowledge', so proficiency in segmenting supports success in spelling simple words. Same-rank direction is justified by this substantive sound-to-spelling dependency rather than by shared grade, code prefix, or the single shared token 'words'. B3.2.2.1 (Sub-Strand 2: Phonics) requires learners to 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write' — foundational grapheme-phoneme correspondence and blending. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 3 Content Standards (same statement-type grain) under Strand 2: Reading, so the comparison is within one strand at rank 2. B3.2.9.1 'Read texts fluently' sits under Sub-Strand 9: Fluency, with source context showing decoding of long texts 'with good pace, accuracy and expression'; B3.2.7.1 'Understand and analyse texts read' sits under Sub-Strand 7: Comprehension and targets meaning-making and analysis of the texts read. This is not mere wording overlap ('read', 'texts'): accurate, well-paced reading of connected text is the enabling processing skill that frees attention for understanding and analysing the same texts, so proficiency in the fluency standard substantively supports success in the comprehension standard. Direction is same-rank and justified by this substantive enabling relation rather than by code order or local rank proximity; the curriculum does not mandate a teaching sequence, and shared Strand/Grade ancestry alone was not treated as evidence. judgment.rationale: Both are Content Standards at the same BASIC 3 rank (2), so direction rests on substantive evidence rather than grade order. B3.2.2.1 (Reading / Phonics) is explicitly encoding-oriented: 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write', i.e. sound-letter correspondence as a means to writing. B3.4.5.1 (Writing / Writing Simple Words and Sentences) targets 'Write accurately using acquired vocabulary and knowledge of grammar', with its continuation rendering reading 'Write accurately using word recognition and knowledge of grammar and vocabulary'. Secure sound-letter mapping and blending underpins accurate spelling and word-level accuracy in sentence writing, so phonics proficiency supports likelihood of success in accurate writing; the reverse dependency is not supported. This is a cross-strand enabling relation, not mere shared-grade or token overlap ('and', 'write'). First (B1.4.3.1.1, Writing / Sub-Strand 3: Writing Letters – Small and Capital) is 'Match lower and upper case letters' — recognising and pairing the small and capital forms of each letter under a standard about using letter-sound knowledge to write legibly. Second (B1.5.1.1.1, Strand 5: Using Writing Conventions / Sub-Strand 1: Using Capitalisation) is 'Write capital letters correctly' under 'Apply knowledge of capitalisation in writing', with a source exemplar describing pick-and-write revision of capital letter writing. judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit under the same BASIC 1 Content Standard B1.2.1.2 'Manipulate the sounds of the letters of English' (Strand 2: Reading, Sub-Strand 1: Pre-Reading Activities), so the pair is judged within one statement-type grain and at equal coordinate rank (BASIC 1, rank 0). The evidence supports a substantive same-rank developmental direction rather than mere repetition: B1.2.1.2.2 requires orally segmenting spoken syllables/words into individual sounds (LC 'Segment syllables/words into sounds'; tags oral, phonemes, segmenting), i.e. isolating discrete phonemes in a word. B1.2.1.2.3 requires saying the new word after deleting, adding or substituting an initial, middle or final sound (LCs for phoneme deletion, addition and substitution), which presupposes the learner can already isolate the target phoneme position within the word and then reassemble the remaining sounds. Proficiency in segmentation therefore supports success in phoneme manipulation, so the source is the segmentation indicator. Shared code prefix, page 39 proximity and the 'sounds' token overlap are only weak nomination signals and were not treated as sufficient on their own. Endpoint evidence carries upstream merge/audit context (including a CONT'D-row merge on the shared Content Standard) and truncated source/LC excerpts for both endpoints; the retained indicator texts and LCs are nevertheless clear and non-conflicting for this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 2 (rank 1) Indicators under the same Reading / Phonics Content Standard B2.2.2.1 ('Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write'), so direction rests on statement substance rather than rank. B2.2.2.1.1 is the narrow generative skill of blending syllables to produce words (LC tags: blending, phonics, syllables, words). B2.2.2.1.2 applies alphabetic knowledge to decode unknown words across a substantially broader set of units - beginning/ending consonants, consonant blends, consonant digraphs, vowel sounds, vowel digraphs and word patterns - evidenced by its six distinct decoding LCs. Reliable syllable blending is the sound-combining operation that supports success at decoding unfamiliar words using these varied letter-sound patterns, so the first indicator builds towards the second; the reverse is not supported because decoding unknown words presupposes rather than enables basic blending.
